description: Somos uma equipe interessada em tecnologia, ciência, análise e visualização de dados. Nosso objetivo é transformar dados em informações relevantes e soluções que possam gerar impacto real. Buscamos pessoas curiosas, criativas e dispostas a colaborar, compartilhar conhecimentos e enfrentar desafios. Acreditamos que, trabalhando juntos, podemos transformar ideias em projetos inovadores e contribuir para um futuro.
summary: SEESAW is a web tool that finds "seesaws" in the Earth system: pairs of regions where the same climate variable is rising in one place and falling in another. Users pick a variable from NASA POWER data (air temperature or precipitation, 1981-2025), see a map of how much it changed per decade across Brazil and its surroundings, and learn where that change is statistically significant. One click on any region searches for its opposite-trending counterpart and produces a plain-language Case File answering the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant. SEESAW addresses the hardest part of the challenge directly: the same variable can trend in opposite directions in different regions under a shared process. This matters because a single regional trend tells only half the story, and because trends that were never tested for significance can mislead decisions about water, farming and energy.
details:
What it does

SEESAW turns a multi-step climate analysis into three clicks. Users choose a variable, explore a honeycomb map of trends per decade, click any cell to open its case, and press "Find my seesaw" to locate regions with a significant opposite trend that also move in anti-phase from year to year. A "Surprise me" button jumps to the strongest case on the map. Every result is summarized in a Case File that can be copied into reports or slides.

How it works

A Python pipeline downloads monthly gridded data from the NASA POWER API (temperature at 2 m and precipitation, 1981-2025) for 1,681 cells of 1 degree covering Brazil and its surroundings. For each cell it computes annual means, the Theil-Sen slope (a robust estimate of change per decade, with a 95% confidence interval) and the Mann-Kendall trend test with trend-free pre-whitening to correct for autocorrelation. It then applies the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across the whole map, so significance holds for the field and not only cell by cell. Users can switch this correction on and off and watch false alarms disappear. Each cell gets one of three verdicts: Significant, Suggestive or Not significant.

The seesaw search runs in the browser. It scores candidate pairs by the strength of their opposite trends and by the negative correlation of their detrended series, which hints at a shared driver. The tool states clearly that this is statistical evidence, not proof of cause.

Benefits and impact

SEESAW applies the significance standards used in climate science and explains the results in plain language, for students, journalists and local planners. With real NASA POWER data, 1,394 of 1,681 cells show a significant temperature trend after correction. Precipitation trends from reanalysis data need extra caution, and the tool's verdicts are designed to make that uncertainty visible instead of hiding it.

Creativity

Most trend tools analyze each region in isolation. SEESAW actively searches for the opposite side of the seesaw, the part of the challenge statement about regions trending in opposite directions under a shared process.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Requests), JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js, GitHub and Vercel. Static site with no backend. Source code: https://github.com/CaioFCSousa/projeto_NASA

Limitations and next steps

Prototype region and two variables; annual means hide seasonal changes; reanalysis is not direct measurement. Next: global coverage, more variables (GRACE water storage, MODIS vegetation, GPM IMERG rainfall), cross-variable seesaws and validation against independent datasets.
